1. Advanced packaging: The top three global providers of advanced packaging (fan-out, wafer-level, and 2.5D/3D integration) are TSMC, Samsung, and Intel. TSMC’s CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) capacity is not publicly disclosed in monthly wafer-equivalent terms, but credible industry estimates for 2024 were in the range of 60,000–70,000 wafers per month, growing to approximately 80,000–90,000 wafers per month by 2026. TSMC distinguishes CoWoS-S (standard), CoWoS-L (large), and CoWoS-R (redistribution only, typically for interposer-less redistribution). Samsung’s competing platform is FOWLP (Fan-Out Wafer Level Packaging) under the “X-Cube” branding, and Intel’s is Foveros (2.5D/3D stacking with embedded die). As of 2026, NVIDIA B200/B300 packaging is constrained by TSMC’s CoWoS capacity, with CoWoS-L being the relevant variant for large reticle designs; Samsung and Intel are not yet able to fully substitute for the high-bandwidth, low-power-delivery requirements of these GPUs.

2. EUV ecosystem: ASML’s low-NA NXE:3800E uses a numerical aperture of ~0.33 and is distinct from the High-NA EXE:5000 (NA ~0.55, first tool shipped in 2023) and EXE:5200 (improved version with larger stage and higher throughput). Customers with High-NA tools installed as of 2025–2026 include Intel (in New Mexico, USA), TSMC (in Taiwan), and Samsung (in South Korea), with limited deployments at a few other IDMs and foundries. EUV pellicle suppliers include ASML (in-house) and Murata Manufacturing; EUV photoresist leaders are ASML (with its proprietary formulations), JSR (now JSR–L), and TOK; EUV mask blanks are dominated by Hoya Corporation (with its subsidiary Hoya Precision Glass) and SCHOTT.

3. HBM stack: SK Hynix has begun volume production of HBM3E and is developing HBM4, with HBM4 expected in 2025–2026 but not yet in high-volume production; Samsung has had HBM3E in production but has faced yield issues with its HBM4 prototypes, leading to delays. Micron’s HBM3E is on track for 2025–2026, with HBM4 likely following in 2026–2027. For 2026, NVIDIA B200/B300 are qualified with HBM3E from SK Hynix and Samsung, with B300 moving toward HBM4 sampling; AMD MI325X is qualified with HBM3E, while MI350/MI400 are not yet publicly qualified with any HBM4 in 2026. HBM bit-share among the three suppliers is approximately: SK Hynix ~50%, Samsung ~30%, and Micron ~20%, though exact figures are not publicly disclosed.

4. EDA and IP under export controls: As of 2025–2026, the US BIS restricts the sale of advanced EDA tools (including Synopsys’ IC Compiler II and PrimeTime, Cadence’s Genus and Innovus, and Siemens’ Tessent and Calibre) for use in China targeting advanced nodes (below 18nm or specific GAAFET restrictions). Indigenous Chinese EDA alternatives include Huawei’s EDA Suite and Shanghai-based Zuoyou (formerly Real-Thread), with realistic node coverage up to 28nm for digital design and limited capability at advanced nodes; no tool currently covers 3nm or even 7nm GAAFET with full signoff. ARM IP licenses are not directly subject to the same BIS restrictions as EDA tools, but any ARM design that incorporates US-controlled “foundational” technology may be subject to end-use/end-user restrictions, and license approvals remain subject to US government review.

5. Specialty materials at advanced nodes: High-purity quartz is dominated by Shin-Etsu Chemical (Japan) and Heraeus (Germany), with Spruce Pine, North Carolina, being a key US quartz source; supply disruptions in 2024–2026 have been reported due to geopolitical tensions and transportation constraints. Specialty gases include NF3 (Air Products, Linde), WF6 (Air Products, Linde, and Coregas), and hexachlorodisilane (Sigma-Aldrich/Merck); supply risks exist due to energy costs and transport. CMP slurries are led by Cabot Microchemical (US) and Saint-Gobain (France); photoresist precursors are supplied by companies like JSR and TOK. No major, publicly confirmed 2024–2026 supply disruptions have been reported for these specific materials at the scale to halt production, but energy and logistics pressures persist.

6. CHIPS Act in practice: Three announced US fab projects with grant amounts are: (i) Intel Ohio (New Albany) — $3.2 billion for two fabs, recipient Intel, location Ohio, with partial disbursement by 2026; (ii) TSMC Arizona (Phoenix) — $6.6 billion for a 3nm/2nm fab, recipient TSMC, location Arizona, with disbursements ongoing through 2026; (iii) Samsung Texas (Taylor) — $6.9 billion for a Texas fab, recipient Samsung, location Texas, with disbursements ongoing and some milestones tied to local content. Clawback or milestone triggers have been invoked in cases where projects fail to meet job-creation or investment commitments, though specific public enforcement actions as of 2026 are limited and case-by-case.
